Copper Quarterly October 2011 

# Executive Summary 

## Funds out, fundamentals in 



- Financial turbulence has driven increased commodity price volatility since mid-September. **Uncertainty about the Eurozone debt crisis and a deteriorating outlook for the US economy dominated the discussions during LME Week** .  In our base case, these storm clouds lead to a dent, but no meltdown, in global economic growth and therefore copper consumption. 



- **We forecast that the market in 2011 and 2012 will be in deficit by 300,000t in both years, with prices back above $9,000/t by Q2 next year** .  We reach this conclusion as with relatively low stock levels throughout the supply chain, scrap market support and modest growth in supply in 2012, copper is unlikely to suffer a repeat of the 2008/09 losses. 



- **Lean inventories throughout the supply chain** , along with broadly stable exchange stocks, **mean that we see no excess inventories of either concentrate, cathode or semis** overhanging the market and threatening a round of cathode destocking.  In addition, **scrap merchants are withholding material** from the market following the 25% cathode price correction.  Scrap discounts have already narrowed and we expect consumers to replace the copper units supplied by this scrap with cathode, **thus supporting refined demand and the price** . 



- **Downward revisions to 2011 refined consumption** , in light of macroeconomic developments, have not been as large as the changes to economic indicators owing to support from scrap replacement.  We have also **reduced our estimate for refined production this year** due to high levels of mine disruptions, which **leads to our forecast of a 300,000t deficit** . 



- We foresee modest growth in mine and refined supply next year.  Thus, **in 2012 the market faces another 300,000t deficit** and stocks falling to minimal levels, helping to drive **the price back above $9,000/t.** The long awaited increase in mine supply from new projects will be met by a recovery in consumption and we expect a **balanced market in 2013** . **Stocks remaining at low levels and a recovery in risk appetite** in the financial sector mean **that prices will rise to over $10,000/t in 2013** . 



- **In 2014-2016, 300,000t/y surpluses emerge** , as the bulge in mine projects comes through and leads to unprecedented growth in mine and refined production. **Prices will ease in response but remain above $9,000/t** throughout the period.

For 2011, global consumption is 100,000t below levels three months ago. Lower growth in 2012 leaves consumption down by 270,000t, compared to July. A recovery in 2013 leads to the gap narrowing to 235,000t in 2013 and to only 130,000t by 2015. **Supply** : Mine disruptions and project delays have resulted in a lowering of our refined production estimate for 2011 by 100,000t compared to previous forecasts. The reduction widens to 380,000t in 2012. Higher output from the bunching of delayed mine projects results in the gap falling to 160,000t in 2013 and being the same as in July in 2014-2015. **Prices** : Given the correction in September, prices for 2011 have been lowered by $680/t and by $380/t in 2012 mainly due to a lower Q1. Sustained low stocks and recovering consumption in 2013 pushes the price to $425/t more than in July. Thereafter, emerging surpluses mean prices fall back in line with previous forecasts by 2015. ### Fear fuels fund flight Financial turbulence has driven increased commodity price volatility since mid-September. The 3-month copper price on the LME fell to a low of $6,760/t on 5th October and traded in a $7,1007,600/t range through to 13th October. Market fundamentals gave few warnings of this impending price correction. Copper demand growth held up well through the summer, with our latest estimate showing a 3% increase for 2011. Exchange stocks have remained stable, while mine production has experienced disruptions from ore grade declines, strikes and extreme weather. All these conditions have been, and continue to be, supportive of higher prices. The price succumbed to fears over how the Eurozone crisis will be resolved and a deteriorating outlook for the US economy, with copper and other “risky” assets taking a knock as investors withdrew into safer assets such as the US dollar (see the chart below). This was notable during LME Week, as copper consumers and producers were more sanguine about the price than financial players. High flying copper dragged back into

During a crisis people look to history for parallels, with many now making comparisons to the 2008 financial crisis for clues to how this latest economic storm may turn out. However, history never truly repeats itself but, as the saying attributed to Mark Twain says, it does rhyme. Our base case macroeconomic forecast calls for a hit to (but no meltdown in) global economic growth from the Eurozone debt crisis. As a result, we believe that the copper market will avoid a further downward correction in the price and actually bounce back to new highs for four key reasons: - Relatively low current stock levels throughout the supply chain - Scrap market offset support - Modest growth in mine and refined supply in 2012 - Currency effects Table II: The short term outlook for the refined copper market |**World Position (''000 tonnes)**|**Q4 11**|**2011 **|**Q1 12 **|**Q2 12 **|**Q3 12 **|**Q4 12**|**2012 **|**Q1 13 **|**Q2 13 **|**Q3 13 **|**Q4 13**|**2013**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |World Production|4616|**18786**|4616|4748|4874|4947|**19185**|4985|5113|5198|5350|**20646**| |World Consumption|4803|**19102**|4744|4982|4840|4930|**19497**|4959|5234|5195|5272|**20660**| |**World S/D Balance**|**(187)**|**(316)**|**(128)**|**(234)**|**34**|**17**|**(311)**|**25**|**(120)**|**2**|**78**|**(14)**| |**SRB est. & reported SHFE**||||||||||||| |**bonded stock chg**

The copper stock pipeline remains very lean across the entire supply chain with little threat of destocking. Inventories of both concentrates and cathode have been drawn down this year particularly in China, where we believe there was a build up in stock by the end of 2010. Consumers around the world have been very reluctant to take any more metal than really needed given the clouded outlook for end-use requirements and tight credit conditions. In addition, exchange stocks at the end of Q3 had risen by only 26,000t on Q2 and 114,000t y-o-y, amounting to only 1.8 weeks of world consumption. Given the opacity of data in the country, China is the big unknown for all things copper, and in particular stock levels. Our analysis and data indicate that, as China’s refined and semis production capacity has grown to feed its consumption requirements, working inventories of cathode at both producers and consumers have increased alongside. In addition, merchants selling material into China have also increased their working stocks at warehouses (mainly bonded, i.e. VAT not yet paid). In total, at the end of Q3 we estimate that there were almost 2Mt of cathode in China, as the table below shows, split roughly between the SRB and other stockholders. These market stocks totalled over 1.0Mt at the end of Q3 2011.

This is down from 1.2Mt at the end of 2010 as the introduction of tighter monetary controls by the government in April this year led to a change in Chinese import regulations.  This restricted the use of copper as collateral for credit purposes and we understand that these speculative inventories were largely drawn down through 2011.  This accounts for the majority of the cumulative 175,000t reduction in off-warrant stocks so far in 2011, according to our estimates.  The net decline in SHFE stocks also helped feed the over 200,000t Q1-Q3 deficit in China.  In our view the remaining non-SRB stocks of 1Mt are reasonable given the copper market in China represents over 40% of global consumption. 

### ...and limited scrap will support refined demand in Q4 2011 

Lessons have been learned by the scrap industry from the 2008/2009 crash in copper prices.  It is now much more difficult to renege on scrap contracts due to the high deposits required up front, particularly from Chinese scrap merchants buying in the USA and elsewhere.  We would expect that in the short term any merchants holding scrap bought at higher prices will keep this material off the market in the hope prices will recover or at least until they feel prices will not do so, at which point they will then have to accept the loss.  In the mean time, those copper units that would have been supplied from this scrap held off the market will be replaced, either directly by cathode (for no.1 scrap by semi fabricators) or indirectly by concentrate (for lower grade material used by smelters).  We have already seen scrap discounts narrow, with Chinese no. 1 scrap reported to be

at a premium to cathode.  Therefore, we expect scrap market dynamics to provide support to refined demand and prices in Q4 2011 and into 2012, as scrap merchants adjust to the price correction. 

Given the uncertainty on the macroeconomic front, we believe that consumers will remain cautious and wait as long as possible before they commit to volumes for their 2012 contracts with the producers.  As for next year’s benchmark cathode premiums, these are most likely to be set at slightly lower levels than were set for this year. 

Despite the deterioration in the prospects for developed world economies, we forecast a 300,000t deficit in refined copper this year.  We have revised down our consumption forecasts to reflect the latest CRU macroeconomic outlook.  However, the downward revisions to refined consumption have not been as large as the changes to the economic indicators, owing to support from scrap replacement.  The exception is in the USA, where Russian rod imports are depressing US refined consumption, irrespective of the economic outlook.  On the other hand, Japan is recovering this year slightly faster than we anticipated.  The developing countries of the world remain robust, supported by infrastructure development whic

h is typically large governmentfunded projects. China and the other BRIC’s (India, Brazil, Russia) are still growing and oil money in the GCC means the countries in this region are still investing, particularly Saudi Arabia. Moreover, copper’s key end-use market, wire and cable, has diverse applications and we do not expect this market to be derailed. Currently, the LME copper price is around 25% less than on 1st August, which will be a big factor supporting consumption in price sensitive markets (China, India, Brazil). Indeed, it can be argued that this is a good time to buy wire and cable. Alongside this relatively positive consumption outlook, we have reduced our estimate for refined production this year due to high levels of mine disruptions, thus leading to the 300,000t deficit. We estimate that the bulk of this year’s deficit has already occurred in China. As outlined earlier, inventories built up over the past two years were run down to feed the shortfall. Following the opening of the arbitrage window net refined imports in China reached 235,000t in August, their highest level so far this year. As China has resumed imports, we expect a deficit to emerge in the world ex-China in Q4 2011. The ongoing problem of declining ore grades and infrastructure constraints, especially in Zambia and Chile, will not be overcome quickly. In addition, some of the recent labour disruptions were related to demands for better working conditions, rather than attempts to secure a larger share of mine profits, so will not be resolved by a lower price. Resource nationalism also remains a key threat for producers, particularly in places like Peru, Mongolia and the DRC where many of the new projects are due to come on stream. As a result of all these factors, we have revised mine production from existing operations down by over 250,000t in 2012 compared to our July Quarterly, with an additional 100,000t from project delays. Consumption growth next year has also been lowered to take account of the change in the macroeconomic outlook, particularly in Europe, the USA and Other Asia (ex-China and Japan). In Japan, the recovery from the earthquake and tsunami means growth will be 4.5% in 2012. Overall, we project that constrained refined production growth will just match the increase in consumption, leaving the market facing another 300,000t deficit. This will lead to stocks falling to minimal levels and help prices recover. Our base case macroeconomic outlook calls for a “muddle through” resolution of the Eurozone crisis, which once it becomes apparent should see an increase in investor confidence and lead to financial inflows into copper. In our view, these fundamental and financial effects will push copper prices back above $9,000/t by Q2 2012 and see them average over that level for the year as a whole. ### Surpluses to develop, but with only a modest stock build In 2013 we forecast that the latest economic wobble will be behind us, by which time we expect the long anticipated increase in mine production from new projects will come through. We therefore predict refined production will rise by 1.5Mt or 7.6% in 2013. This growth in supply will lift the constraint on refined consumption, which we anticipate will respond by increasing by 6.0%. With supply outpacing demand, the market will move into balance, but stocks will remain at low levels. In reaction, we see prices rising to an average of $10,500/t in Q2 2013 and averaging just over $10,000/t for the whole year. |Table IV: World refine|d cop

Refined consumption growth will also increase strongly in that time frame but at a slightly lower rate, matching the increase in global industrial production. The slight divergence in growth between refined production and consumption will see 300,000+t/y surpluses emerging in the final three years of the outlook period and a build in exchange inventories. However, the build will be relatively modest and by 2016 inventories will only reach levels on a par with the end of 2009. Copper prices will ease in response but remain above $9,000/t throughout the period. ### Currency effects to keep Chinese prices down... In part we expect to see copper prices recovering to and exceeding the 2011 highs as the effect of currency movements on copper prices in different countries will support the shift of consumption away from industrialised countries to emerging markets over the next five years. China is a particularly price sensitive market and we forecast that the appreciation in the RMB will fully offset our forecast rise in LME prices next year, leaving LME prices converted into RMB averaging the same as in 2011, as the chart on the following page shows. Furthermore, in RMB terms the increase in copper prices in 2013 will be to a quarterly peak below the all-time high achieved in Q1 2011. Subsequent appreciation will lead to prices in RMB falling to 10% below 2011 levels by 2016. Although prices in 2012 and 2013 in China will rise, they will remain below all-time highs, which means that consumption growth in the world’s largest consumer will not be as negatively impacted as in other countries. ### ...but boost prices even higher in Europe and Japan At the other end of the scale (see the chart), in 2013 we expect Japanese and European copper consumers to face prices 30% and 20% higher than the average 2011 price, respectively. With the depreciation moderating, yen copper prices are then forecast to track LME prices lower. A continually weakening euro, however, will see European prices 16% above 2011 levels in 2016. Such sustained high prices will weigh on copper consumption growth, as Japanese and European semis producers struggle to maintain international competitiveness. In fact, at 1.5% and 1.6% respectively, we forecast that Western Europe and Japan w

ill see the slowest average growth in refined consumption among major consuming regions over the next five years. Macroeconomic and financial risks and their consequent impact on consumption are largely offset by the risk of lower refined production. By 2013, however, the challenges facing the copper mining industry in achieving the rapid 7.6% growth forecast for refined output in the base case more than offsets the other risks and pushes the high side to 45% ab

ove that of the downside. Conversely, further out in the forecast period, as deficits turn into surpluses and stocks are forecast to be rebuilt, the risks move back to a more balanced position. By 2016, the upside is only 10% greater than the downside. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly October 2011 Executive Summary 9 #### Macroeconomic and financial risks The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the current financial market turmoil will play out, both in terms of the direct impact of financial players on the copper price and the indirect effects of a financial crisis in Europe on the wider economy and on refined consumption. We believe that the Eurozone crisis has two possible outcomes. Either, Greece restructures its debt and defaults in an orderly way (our base case), or the default is disorderly and sparks another financial crisis. The latter would push industrialised countries back into recession and lead to a lower average price in 2012 than that achieved in 2011. The market currently believes global manufacturing activity will enter a soft patch in 2012. However, there is an upside risk that once forecasters start to revise their forecasts up as the future begins to look brighter speculators will buy well ahead of a decisive turnaround in lagging data. The next meeting of EU policymakers during the first week of November will be critical to setting market perceptions going into 2012. #### Production risks All production risks are to the upside. The first is that, should financial market stress lead to a double dip recession in the Eurozone and the USA, financing for mine projects due on stream over the next five years would likely be affected, leading to further delays. Even the majors, who are flush with cash, may ramp up their projects more slowly or otherwise defer some of the production due on stream from their projects. Even if a financial crisis is avoided, insufficient availability of equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge and we believe that there is a much greater downside than upside risk to our production forecast. The other significant production risk to the outlook is that any shortage of scrap during a recession (due to weaker generation) would lead to lower smelter production and an increased reliance on scarce concentrates. Although the emerging markets are performing well, driven by domestic demand, there are concerns about inflationary pressures. Copper consumption would be negatively affected by governments introducing anti-inflationary policies which would dent economic growth. 

Longer term, the substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth, with CRU forecasting the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium averaging close to 4:1 in 2013 and 3.7:1 over the period from 2012 to 2016. 

#### **Upside** 

The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) would lead to additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 

Any double-dip would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic growth further from the industrialised countries, by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 

At lower prices some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of currency appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away from the dollar and directly into commodity investments as a means of diversification.
